\documentclass[10pt,a4paper]{article}
\usepackage[draft]{tcdoc}
%% Tables are placed with [H] so each sits under the prose that explains it.
\usepackage{float}

%% The two wide tables run in landscape. pdflscape rather than lscape so the PDF
%% carries a /Rotate on those pages and a viewer shows them the right way up
%% without the reader turning their head. Inside the environment \textwidth
%% becomes the portrait \textheight, so the block goes from 182 mm to 261 mm --
%% which is what makes a ten-column table legible instead of a hyphenation stack.
\usepackage{pdflscape}

%% Ragged-right p column. Justifying a 25 mm column stretches interword space and
%% forces two or three hyphenations per line; ragged right is what a dense table
%% actually wants. \arraybackslash restores \\ after the > directive eats it.
\newcolumntype{L}[1]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{#1}}

\title{\vspace{-1.5em}One Hundred Fifty-six Candidates for Datasets 50--200}
\author{Michael Volk}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\thispagestyle{empty}

\noindent
The database holds 49 schematized and L0--L4-verified \org{Saccharomyces cerevisiae}
datasets. Reaching 200 needs 151 more. Table~\ref{tab:candidates} ranks 156 candidates and
Table~\ref{tab:sources} gives each one's citation, link and data location; rows 1--151 are
the recommended set and the remaining 5 are a ranked reserve. Table~\ref{tab:excluded}
records what was considered and dropped, which is where the one hard constraint shows up:
a dataset earns a place only if the total genomic content of each strain can be
reconstructed.
